title: Testamentary capacity disputes - proving a will was validly made
p1:
A signature on a will does not always mean the will is legally valid.

Sometimes, the biggest battle begins after a person has passed away: was the person truly capable of making that decision?
p2:
Many believe that memory loss or old age automatically invalidates a will. That is not true.

A person can still make a valid will if they understand what they are doing, know what property they have, and understand who may have a claim on their estate.
p3:
In testamentary capacity disputes, courts often look beyond medical labels. They examine evidence like conversations, medical records, witness statements, and the person’s actions around the time the will was created.

The surprising part? A diagnosis alone may not prove incapacity. The key question is whether the person understood the specific decision they were making when the will was signed.

A valid will is not just about a signature. It is about proving the person’s intention and understanding at that moment.
conclusion: Do you think a medical diagnosis should automatically affect the validity of a will, or should the person’s actual understanding at the time matter more?
